blocks.body:
Which primes are sums of two squares? Small cases suggest a pattern: $2 = 1^2+1^2$, $5 = 1^2+2^2$, $13 = 2^2+3^2$, $17 = 1^2+4^2$, $29 = 2^2+5^2$, while $3, 7, 11, 19, 23$ are not sums of two squares at all. Fermat stated the rule: an odd prime is a sum of two squares exactly when it leaves remainder $1$ on division by $4$.

The key is to factor: $a^2+b^2 = (a+bi)(a-bi)$ is a product in a larger number system, the Gaussian integers. Once we know that this ring has unique factorization, just like $\mathbb Z$, the question "is $p$ a sum of two squares?" becomes "does $p$ stay prime in the larger ring?", and that question has a clean answer.

blocks.title: Gaussian integers
blocks.body:
The Gaussian integers are the complex numbers $\mathbb Z[i] = \{a+bi : a, b \in \mathbb Z\}$, where $i^2 = -1$. They are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, since $(a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i$.

Geometrically, $\mathbb Z[i]$ is the square grid of points with integer coordinates in the complex plane.

blocks.title: Norm
blocks.body:
For $\alpha = a+bi$ the norm is $N(\alpha) = \alpha\bar\alpha = a^2+b^2 = |\alpha|^2$. It is a non-negative integer, it is $0$ only for $\alpha = 0$, and it is multiplicative: $N(\alpha\beta) = N(\alpha)N(\beta)$, because $|\alpha\beta| = |\alpha|\,|\beta|$.

The norm converts statements about Gaussian integers into statements about ordinary integers. In particular, if $\alpha \mid \beta$ in $\mathbb Z[i]$ then $N(\alpha) \mid N(\beta)$ in $\mathbb Z$. Multiplicativity, written out, is the old identity $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) = (ac-bd)^2 + (ad+bc)^2$.

blocks.title: Units, associates and Gaussian primes
blocks.body:
Divisibility works as in $\mathbb Z$: $\alpha \mid \beta$ means $\beta = \alpha\gamma$ for some $\gamma \in \mathbb Z[i]$. A unit is an element that divides $1$. If $uv = 1$ then $N(u)N(v) = 1$, so $N(u) = 1$, and the only integer solutions of $a^2+b^2 = 1$ give the four units $1, -1, i, -i$.

Two elements are associates if one is a unit times the other. Associates divide each other and play the same role, just as $7$ and $-7$ do in $\mathbb Z$. A nonzero $\alpha$ has exactly four associates $\alpha, -\alpha, i\alpha, -i\alpha$: the quarter-turn rotations of $\alpha$.

A Gaussian prime is a nonzero non-unit $\pi$ whose only divisors are units and associates of $\pi$. The norm gives a quick test in one direction: if $N(\alpha)$ is a rational prime, then $\alpha$ is a Gaussian prime. Indeed, if $\alpha = \beta\gamma$ then $N(\beta)N(\gamma) = N(\alpha)$ is prime, so one factor has norm $1$ and is a unit. So $1+i$ (norm $2$), $2+i$ (norm $5$) and $3+2i$ (norm $13$) are Gaussian primes.

Two small experiments. First, $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$, so the rational prime $5$ is not a Gaussian prime. Second, suppose $3 = \beta\gamma$ with neither factor a unit. Then $N(\beta)N(\gamma) = 9$ with both norms greater than $1$, so $N(\beta) = 3$, that is $a^2+b^2 = 3$, which has no integer solutions. So $3$ stays prime in $\mathbb Z[i]$, even though its norm $9$ is not prime. The whole theory is about explaining this difference between $5$ and $3$.

blocks.title: Division with remainder in Z[i]
blocks.body: For any $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb Z[i]$ with $\beta \ne 0$ there are $\kappa, \rho \in \mathbb Z[i]$ with $$\alpha = \kappa\beta + \rho, \qquad N(\rho) \le \tfrac12 N(\beta) < N(\beta).$$

Work in the complex numbers. The quotient $\alpha/\beta = \alpha\bar\beta/N(\beta)$ equals $x + yi$ with $x, y$ rational. Let $m, n$ be integers nearest to $x$ and $y$, so $|x-m| \le \tfrac12$ and $|y-n| \le \tfrac12$. Put $\kappa = m + ni$ and $\rho = \alpha - \kappa\beta$. Then $\rho$ is a Gaussian integer, and $\rho = \beta\bigl((x-m) + (y-n)i\bigr)$, so
$$N(\rho) = |\beta|^2\bigl((x-m)^2 + (y-n)^2\bigr) \le N(\beta)\Bigl(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14\Bigr) = \tfrac12 N(\beta).$$
Geometrically: every point of the plane lies within distance $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ of a grid point, and multiplying by $\beta$ scales distances by $|\beta|$.

blocks.title: Unique factorization in Z[i]
blocks.body: Every nonzero non-unit of $\mathbb Z[i]$ is a product of Gaussian primes, and this factorization is unique apart from the order of the factors and replacing factors by associates.

Existence, by induction on the norm: if $\alpha$ is not prime, write $\alpha =  eta\gamma$ with $ eta, \gamma$ non-units. Then $1 < N( eta), N(\gamma) < N(\alpha)$, so $ eta$ and $\gamma$ are already products of primes.

For uniqueness we need Euclid's lemma: if a Gaussian prime $\pi$ divides $\alpha eta$, then $\pi \mid \alpha$ or $\pi \mid  eta$. Let $S = \{\mu\pi + 
u\alpha : \mu, 
u \in \mathbb Z[i]\}$ and choose a nonzero $\delta \in S$ of smallest norm. Divide $\pi$ by $\delta$: the remainder $\pi - \kappa\delta$ again lies in $S$ and has smaller norm than $\delta$, so it is $0$ and $\delta \mid \pi$. In the same way $\delta \mid \alpha$. As $\pi$ is prime, $\delta$ is a unit or an associate of $\pi$. Suppose $\pi 
mid \alpha$. Then $\delta$ cannot be an associate of $\pi$ (that would give $\pi \mid \delta \mid \alpha$), so $\delta$ is a unit, and multiplying by $\delta^{-1}$ gives $1 = \mu\pi + 
u\alpha$ for some $\mu, 
u$. Multiply by $ eta$: $ eta = \mu\pi eta + 
u\alpha eta$, and $\pi$ divides both terms on the right, so $\pi \mid  eta$.

Now let $\pi_1\cdots\pi_r = \pi'_1\cdots\pi'_s$ be two factorizations into primes. By Euclid's lemma $\pi_1$ divides some $\pi'_j$, so it is an associate of $\pi'_j$. Cancel the two (absorbing a unit into another factor) and repeat. This is word for word the argument for $\mathbb Z$ in [[fta]], with the norm playing the role of absolute value.

blocks.title: How rational primes factor in Z[i]
blocks.body:
Every Gaussian prime divides exactly one rational prime $p$, and the rational primes factor as follows.

1. $p = 2$: $2 = -i(1+i)^2$, a unit times the square of the prime $1+i$ ($2$ ramifies).
2. $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$: $p = \pi\bar\pi$ with $\pi = a+bi$, $N(\pi) = p$, and $\pi$, $\bar\pi$ are non-associate Gaussian primes ($p$ splits).
3. $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$: $p$ remains a Gaussian prime, of norm $p^2$ ($p$ is inert).

Up to associates, these are all the Gaussian primes. In particular
$$p = a^2+b^2 = (a+bi)(a-bi) \text{ is solvable} \iff p \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \ \text{or}\ p = 2.$$

A Gaussian prime $\pi$ divides $\pi\bar\pi = N(\pi)$, a positive integer. Factor $N(\pi)$ into rational primes; by Euclid's lemma $\pi$ divides one of them, say $p$. It cannot divide a second prime $q \ne p$: writing $1 = up + vq$ with integers $u, v$ would give $\pi \mid 1$. From $\pi \mid p$ we get $N(\pi) \mid N(p) = p^2$, so $N(\pi) = p$ or $N(\pi) = p^2$. In the second case $p/\pi$ has norm $1$, so $p$ is an associate of $\pi$ and is itself prime.

$p = 2$: $(1+i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i$, hence $-i(1+i)^2 = -i \cdot 2i = 2$.

$p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$: every square is $0$ or $1$ mod $4$, so $a^2 + b^2 \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and no Gaussian integer has norm $p$. Hence every prime factor of $p$ has norm $p^2$, and $p$ is prime.

$p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$: by Euler's criterion $-1$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$ (see [[quadratic-residues]]), so there is an integer $m$ with $p \mid m^2 + 1 = (m+i)(m-i)$. But $p$ divides neither factor, because $(m \pm i)/p = m/p \pm i/p$ is not a Gaussian integer. By Euclid's lemma $p$ is not a Gaussian prime, so it has a prime factor $\pi = a + bi$ of norm $p$, and $p = a^2 + b^2 = \pi\bar\pi$. Since $\pi$ divides $(m+i)(m-i)$ it divides one factor; swapping $\pi$ and $\bar\pi$ if necessary, $\pi \mid m+i$, and by conjugation $\bar\pi \mid m - i$. If $\pi$ and $\bar\pi$ were associates, $\pi$ would divide both $m+i$ and $m-i$, hence their difference $2i$, and then $p = N(\pi)$ would divide $N(2i) = 4$, which is absurd.

Finally, every Gaussian prime divides some rational prime, so it is an associate of one of the primes found above. And $p = a^2 + b^2$ says precisely that $p$ is the norm of a Gaussian integer, which happens for $p = 2$ and $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and never for $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

blocks.title: Counting representations
blocks.body:
Unique factorization gives more than existence. If $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $p = \pi\bar\pi$, the Gaussian integers of norm $p$ are exactly the eight numbers $u\pi$ and $u\bar\pi$ with $u$ a unit. So the representation $p = a^2 + b^2$ is unique apart from the order and the signs of $a$ and $b$.

For general $n$, a Gaussian integer $\alpha$ with $N(\alpha) = n$ is assembled prime by prime. Let $e_p$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$.

- For a split prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\alpha$ contains $\pi^j\bar\pi^{\,e_p - j}$ for some $0 \le j \le e_p$: that is $e_p + 1$ choices.
- For an inert prime $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, the norm of $q$ is $q^2$, so $e_q$ must be even and $\alpha$ contains exactly $q^{e_q/2}$: one choice, or none if $e_q$ is odd.
- The prime $2$ contributes $(1+i)^{e_2}$: one choice.
- Finally multiply by one of the $4$ units.

So the number $r_2(n)$ of pairs $(a, b) \in \mathbb Z^2$ with $a^2 + b^2 = n$ is
$$r_2(n) = 4\prod_{p \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)} (e_p + 1)$$
when every prime $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ occurs to an even power in $n$, and $r_2(n) = 0$ otherwise. This is the complete answer to the question in [[sums-of-squares]]. It can be repackaged as $r_2(n) = 4\bigl(d_1(n) - d_3(n)\bigr)$, where $d_j(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$ that are $\equiv j \pmod 4$.

blocks.title: Two ways to write 65
blocks.body: Factor $65$ into Gaussian primes and find all ways of writing $65$ as a sum of two squares.
blocks.solution:
$65 = 5 \cdot 13$ with $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$ and $13 = (3+2i)(3-2i)$, all four factors having prime norm. A Gaussian integer of norm $65$ takes one prime above $5$ and one above $13$, times a unit. Up to units and conjugation there are two essentially different choices:
$$(2+i)(3+2i) = 6 + 4i + 3i + 2i^2 = 4 + 7i, \qquad (2+i)(3-2i) = 6 - 4i + 3i - 2i^2 = 8 - i.$$
Taking norms, $65 = 4^2 + 7^2 = 8^2 + 1^2$. The other choices only change signs and order.

Counting: $r_2(65) = 4 \cdot (1+1)(1+1) = 16$, that is $8$ signed ordered pairs for each of the two representations. Also all four divisors $1, 5, 13, 65$ are $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so $4(d_1 - d_3) = 16$.

blocks.title: Finding the square roots by the Euclidean algorithm
blocks.body: Given that $12^2 = 144 \equiv -1 \pmod{29}$, find integers $a, b$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 29$ without trial and error.
blocks.solution:
From the proof above, the prime $\pi$ of norm $29$ divides both $29$ and $12 + i$, so it is (up to a unit) their greatest common divisor. Run the Euclidean algorithm in $\mathbb Z[i]$.

Divide $29$ by $12+i$: $\dfrac{29}{12+i} = \dfrac{29(12-i)}{145} = \dfrac{12 - i}{5} = 2.4 - 0.2i$, whose nearest Gaussian integer is $2$. The remainder is $29 - 2(12+i) = 5 - 2i$, of norm $29 < 145$.

Divide $12 + i$ by $5 - 2i$: $\dfrac{(12+i)(5+2i)}{29} = \dfrac{60 + 24i + 5i - 2}{29} = \dfrac{58 + 29i}{29} = 2 + i$, with remainder $0$.

So $\gcd(29, 12+i) = 5 - 2i$, and $29 = N(5-2i) = 5^2 + 2^2$. The same computation works for any prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ once a square root of $-1$ mod $p$ is known.

blocks.title: A cube one more than a square
blocks.body: Find all integers $x, y$ with $x^2 + 1 = y^3$.
blocks.solution:
Parity first. If $x$ is odd then $x^2 + 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, so $y$ is even and $y^3 \equiv 0 \pmod 8$, a contradiction. So $x$ is even and $x^2 + 1$ is odd.

Factor in $\mathbb Z[i]$: $(x+i)(x-i) = y^3$. A common divisor $\delta$ of $x+i$ and $x-i$ divides their difference $2i = (1+i)^2$, so $\delta$ is a unit times a power of $1+i$. But $1 + i \nmid x + i$, since otherwise $2 = N(1+i)$ would divide $N(x+i) = x^2+1$, which is odd. So $x + i$ and $x - i$ have no common prime factor.

By unique factorization, each Gaussian prime dividing $y$ occurs in $y^3$ with exponent a multiple of $3$, and all of it sits in just one of the two coprime factors. Hence $x + i = u\gamma^3$ for a unit $u$ and some $\gamma \in \mathbb Z[i]$. Every unit is a cube ($1 = 1^3$, $-1 = (-1)^3$, $i = (-i)^3$, $-i = i^3$), so we may absorb $u$ and write $x + i = (a+bi)^3$. Expanding,
$$(a+bi)^3 = (a^3 - 3ab^2) + (3a^2b - b^3)i,$$
so $b(3a^2 - b^2) = 1$. Then $b = \pm 1$. If $b = 1$ then $3a^2 = 2$, impossible; if $b = -1$ then $3a^2 - 1 = -1$, so $a = 0$. This gives $x = a^3 - 3ab^2 = 0$ and $y = 1$.

The only solution is $(x, y) = (0, 1)$.

blocks.body:
- Uniqueness is only up to units and order. The factorizations $5 = (1+2i)(1-2i)$ and $5 = (2-i)(2+i)$ are the same, since $1 + 2i = i(2-i)$ and $1 - 2i = -i(2+i)$.
- $\pi$ and $\bar\pi$ are different primes for $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, but $1+i$ and $1-i = -i(1+i)$ are associates. That is exactly the difference between splitting and ramifying.
- Unique factorization is not automatic for rings of this shape. In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ one has $6 = 2\cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ with four irreducible, pairwise non-associate factors. What saved $\mathbb Z[i]$ was the division algorithm.

- The failure of unique factorization in rings like $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is repaired by factoring ideals instead of numbers: see [[ideals]]. In that language, the theorem above says that $(2) = (1+i)^2$, $(p) = (\pi)(\bar\pi)$ for $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and $(q)$ is prime for $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
- The same programme with $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$ in place of $i$ gives the [[eisenstein-integers]] and the primes of the form $x^2 + 3y^2$.
- Sums of two squares are the binary quadratic form of discriminant $-4$; see [[quadratic-forms]].
- The counting formula $r_2(n) = 4(d_1(n) - d_3(n))$ is the coefficient form of the identity $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(i)}(s) = \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-4})$ for the [[dedekind-zeta]] function of $\mathbb Q(i)$.
- Biquadratic (fourth-power) reciprocity lives in $\mathbb Z[i]$ the way cubic reciprocity lives in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$.

2. Let $a, b$ be coprime integers. Show that every odd prime factor of $a^2 + b^2$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
3. Using $22^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{97}$ and the Euclidean algorithm in $\mathbb Z[i]$, write $97$ as a sum of two squares.
4. Compute $r_2(325)$ and list all representations of $325$ as $a^2 + b^2$ with $0 \le a \le b$.

blocks.body:
Which primes can be written as $x^2 + 3y^2$? Try a few: $7 = 2^2 + 3\cdot 1^2$, $13 = 1^2 + 3\cdot 2^2$, $19 = 4^2 + 3 \cdot 1^2$, $31 = 2^2 + 3\cdot 3^2$, but $5, 11, 17, 23, 29$ cannot. The pattern is: $p = x^2 + 3y^2$ exactly when $p = 3$ or $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.

As with sums of two squares, the explanation is factorization in a bigger ring. Here the natural ring is not $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ but the slightly larger ring generated by a cube root of unity. It has six units instead of four, its elements form a triangular lattice instead of a square one, and it is the home of cubic reciprocity.

blocks.title: Eisenstein integers
blocks.body:
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3} = \dfrac{-1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$, a root of $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, so $\omega^3 = 1$, $\omega^2 = -1 - \omega$ and $\bar\omega = \omega^2$. The Eisenstein integers are
$$\mathbb Z[\omega] = \{a + b\omega : a, b \in \mathbb Z\}.$$
The relation $\omega^2 = -1-\omega$ shows that products stay in the set: $(a + b\omega)(c + d\omega) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc - bd)\omega$.

$\mathbb Z[\omega]$ is the ring of integers of the field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$: it consists of all numbers in that field that are roots of monic integer polynomials. Its elements form the triangular lattice in the plane. Note that $\sqrt{-3} = 1 + 2\omega$, so $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is a proper subring.

blocks.title: Norm
blocks.body:
For $\alpha = a + b\omega$,
$$N(a + b\omega) = (a + b\omega)(a + b\bar\omega) = a^2 + ab(\omega + \bar\omega) + b^2\omega\bar\omega = a^2 - ab + b^2,$$
using $\omega + \bar\omega = -1$ and $\omega\bar\omega = 1$. Since $N(\alpha) = |\alpha|^2$ it is multiplicative, and $4N(\alpha) = (2a - b)^2 + 3b^2$, which shows it is positive for $\alpha \ne 0$.

The identity $4N = (2a-b)^2 + 3b^2$ is the bridge between this norm and the form $x^2 + 3y^2$.

blocks.title: Six units
blocks.body:
A unit $u$ satisfies $N(u) = 1$, i.e. $(2a - b)^2 + 3b^2 = 4$. Then $b \in \{0, 1, -1\}$: $b = 0$ gives $a = \pm 1$; $b = 1$ gives $(2a-1)^2 = 1$, so $a \in \{0, 1\}$; $b = -1$ gives $(2a+1)^2 = 1$, so $a \in \{0, -1\}$. The six units are
$$\pm 1, \quad \pm\omega, \quad \pm\omega^2 \ (\text{note } 1 + \omega = -\omega^2),$$
the sixth roots of unity, at the corners of a regular hexagon. Each nonzero element has six associates, obtained by rotating through multiples of $60^\circ$.

How do the coordinates change under rotation? Multiplying by $\omega$ sends $a + b\omega$ to $a\omega + b\omega^2 = -b + (a - b)\omega$. Applying this twice, the second coordinates of $\alpha$, $\omega\alpha$, $\omega^2\alpha$ are $b$, $a - b$, $-a$. We will use this below.

blocks.title: Division with remainder in Z[ω]
blocks.body: For $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $\beta \ne 0$ there are $\kappa, \rho \in \mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $\alpha = \kappa\beta + \rho$ and $N(\rho) \le \tfrac34 N(\beta)$. Consequently $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ has unique factorization into primes, up to order and units.

Write $\alpha/\beta = \alpha\bar\beta/N(\beta) = s + t\omega$ with $s, t$ rational; this is possible because $\alpha\bar\beta \in \mathbb Z[\omega]$. Choose integers $m, n$ with $|s - m| \le \tfrac12$, $|t - n| \le \tfrac12$, put $\kappa = m + n\omega$ and $\rho = \alpha - \kappa\beta = \beta\,(u + v\omega)$ with $u = s - m$, $v = t - n$. For real $u, v$ we still have $|u + v\omega|^2 = u^2 - uv + v^2$, so
$$N(\rho) = N(\beta)\,(u^2 - uv + v^2) \le N(\beta)\Bigl(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac14\Bigr) = \tfrac34 N(\beta).$$

Unique factorization now follows exactly as in $\mathbb Z$ (see [[fta]], or the parallel argument for [[gaussian-integers]]): division with remainder gives, for a prime $\pi$ not dividing $\alpha$, elements $\mu, \nu$ with $\mu\pi + \nu\alpha = 1$; this gives Euclid's lemma ($\pi \mid \alpha\beta \Rightarrow \pi \mid \alpha$ or $\pi \mid \beta$); and Euclid's lemma gives uniqueness.

blocks.title: The special prime 1 − ω
blocks.body:
Let $\lambda = 1 - \omega$. Then $N(\lambda) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, so $\lambda$ is prime, and
$$\lambda^2 = 1 - 2\omega + \omega^2 = 1 - 2\omega - 1 - \omega = -3\omega, \qquad\text{so}\qquad 3 = -\omega^2\lambda^2.$$
The rational prime $3$ is a unit times the square of a prime: it ramifies, just like $2 = -i(1+i)^2$ in $\mathbb Z[i]$.

Since $\omega \equiv 1 \pmod\lambda$, every $a + b\omega$ is congruent to the integer $a + b$ modulo $\lambda$, and since $3$ is divisible by $\lambda$, every element is congruent to exactly one of $0, 1, -1$ modulo $\lambda$. The residue ring $\mathbb Z[\omega]/(\lambda)$ is the field with three elements.

blocks.title: Primes of Z[ω]

blocks.body:
As for the Gaussian integers, a prime $\pi$ divides $N(\pi) = \pi\bar\pi$, hence divides exactly one rational prime $p$, and $N(\pi) \in \{p, p^2\}$; if $N(\pi) = p^2$ then $p$ is an associate of $\pi$ and stays prime. The case $p = 3$ was done above.

$q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$: from $4N = (2a - b)^2 + 3b^2$ we get $N \equiv 4N \equiv (2a - b)^2 \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 3$. So no element has norm $q$, and $q$ stays prime.

$p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$: by quadratic reciprocity $\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right) = \left(\frac{p}{3}\right) = 1$ (see [[quadratic-residues]]), so $m^2 \equiv -3 \pmod p$ for some integer $m$. Then
$$p \mid m^2 + 3 = (m + \sqrt{-3})(m - \sqrt{-3}) = (m + 1 + 2\omega)(m - 1 - 2\omega),$$
but $p$ divides neither factor, since the coefficient $\pm 2/p$ of $\omega$ in the quotient is not an integer. So $p$ is not prime in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and has a prime factor $\pi$ of norm $p$, giving $p = \pi\bar\pi$. As $\pi$ divides one of the two factors, we may choose $\pi \mid m + \sqrt{-3}$ and then $\bar\pi \mid m - \sqrt{-3}$. If $\pi$ and $\bar\pi$ were associates, $\pi$ would divide the difference $2\sqrt{-3}$, so $p$ would divide $N(2\sqrt{-3}) = 12$, impossible for $p \ge 7$.

Finally the representations. We have shown that a prime $p$ is a norm $a^2 - ab + b^2$ exactly when $p = 3$ or $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. If $p = N(\pi)$ with $\pi = a + b\omega$, at least one of the second coordinates $b$, $a - b$, $-a$ of the associates $\pi, \omega\pi, \omega^2\pi$ is even: if $b$ or $a$ is even then $b$ or $-a$ is, and if both are odd then $a - b$ is even. Taking that associate, with $b = 2c$,
$$p = a^2 - 2ac + 4c^2 = (a - c)^2 + 3c^2.$$
Conversely $x^2 + 3y^2 = N\bigl((x + y) + 2y\omega\bigr)$, since $(x+y) + 2y\omega = x + y\sqrt{-3}$.

blocks.title: Factoring 7, 13 and 21
blocks.body: Factor $7$, $13$ and $21$ into primes of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$.
blocks.solution:
We need $a^2 - ab + b^2 = 7$: $a = 3$, $b = 1$ gives $9 - 3 + 1 = 7$. With $\overline{3 + \omega} = 3 + \omega^2 = 2 - \omega$,
$$(3 + \omega)(2 - \omega) = 6 - 3\omega + 2\omega - \omega^2 = 6 - \omega - \omega^2 = 7.$$
For $13$: $a = 4$, $b = 1$ gives $16 - 4 + 1 = 13$, and $13 = (4 + \omega)(3 - \omega)$.

For $21 = 3 \cdot 7$: $21 = -\omega^2(1-\omega)^2(3+\omega)(2-\omega)$.

To read off $7 = x^2 + 3y^2$: for $3 + \omega$ the second coordinates of the associates are $1$, $3 - 1 = 2$, $-3$. The even one belongs to $\omega(3 + \omega) = -1 + 2\omega$, so $c = 1$ and $7 = (-1 - 1)^2 + 3\cdot 1^2 = 4 + 3$.

blocks.title: Splitting 31 with the Euclidean algorithm
blocks.body: Given $11^2 = 121 \equiv -3 \pmod{31}$, find a prime of norm $31$ in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and write $31 = x^2 + 3y^2$.
blocks.solution:
A prime above $31$ divides $31$ and $11 + \sqrt{-3} = 12 + 2\omega$, so take their gcd.

Step 1: $\dfrac{31}{12 + 2\omega} = \dfrac{5}{2} - \dfrac12\omega$ (check: $(12 + 2\omega)(5 - \omega) = 60 + 10\omega - 12\omega - 2\omega^2 = 62$). Round to $\kappa = 2$; the remainder is $31 - 2(12 + 2\omega) = 7 - 4\omega$, of norm $49 + 28 + 16 = 93 < 124 = N(12+2\omega)$.

Step 2: $\dfrac{12 + 2\omega}{7 - 4\omega} = \dfrac43 + \dfrac23\omega$; round to $\kappa = 1 + \omega$. Since $(1 + \omega)(7 - 4\omega) = 11 + 7\omega$, the remainder is $(12 + 2\omega) - (11 + 7\omega) = 1 - 5\omega$, of norm $1 + 5 + 25 = 31$.

Step 3: $7 - 4\omega = (2 + \omega)(1 - 5\omega)$, remainder $0$.

So $\pi = 1 - 5\omega$ has norm $31$. Its associates have second coordinates $-5$, $1 - (-5) = 6$, $-1$; the even one belongs to $\omega\pi = 5 + 6\omega$, giving $c = 3$ and $31 = (5 - 3)^2 + 3\cdot 3^2 = 4 + 27$.

blocks.title: Prime factors of n² + n + 1
blocks.body: Show that every prime factor of $n^2 + n + 1$ is $3$ or $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$, and deduce that there are infinitely many primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$.
blocks.solution:
In $\mathbb Z[\omega]$, $n^2 + n + 1 = (n - \omega)(n - \bar\omega) = N(n - \omega)$. If a prime $q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ divided $N(n - \omega) = (n - \omega)(n - \bar\omega)$, then since $q$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ it would divide $n - \omega$ or $n - \bar\omega$; but $(n - \omega)/q$ has $\omega$-coefficient $-1/q$, not an integer (and similarly for $n - \bar\omega = n + 1 + \omega$). So $q \nmid n^2 + n + 1$. (An elementary version: $4(n^2 + n + 1) = (2n+1)^2 + 3$, so $p \mid n^2 + n + 1$ with $p > 3$ makes $-3$ a quadratic residue mod $p$, forcing $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.)

Now suppose $p_1, \dots, p_k$ were all the primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Let $n = 3p_1\cdots p_k$ and $M = n^2 + n + 1 > 1$. Then $M \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ and $M \equiv 1 \pmod{p_j}$, so no prime factor of $M$ is $3$ or any $p_j$. But all prime factors of $M$ are $3$ or $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$, a contradiction.

For example, $n = 3\cdot 7 = 21$ gives $M = 463$, a prime $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$ not on the list.

blocks.body:
- $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is the wrong ring: there $4 = 2\cdot 2 = (1 + \sqrt{-3})(1 - \sqrt{-3})$ with all factors irreducible. The fix is to include $\omega = (-1 + \sqrt{-3})/2$.
- There are six units, not four. Statements "unique up to sign" from $\mathbb Z[i]$ become "unique up to the six units".
- Some books write elements as $a - b\omega$ or use $\omega^2$ as the generator, so the norm appears as $a^2 + ab + b^2$; it takes the same values as $a^2 - ab + b^2$.
- $3$ does not split: $3 = -\omega^2(1 - \omega)^2$ ramifies, so $\lambda$ and $\bar\lambda = 1 - \omega^2 = -\omega^2\lambda$ are associates.
- The splitting rule is about $p \bmod 3$, not $p \bmod 4$; for instance $13$ splits in both $\mathbb Z[i]$ and $\mathbb Z[\omega]$, while $7$ splits only in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$.

- For a prime $\pi$ with $N(\pi) = p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the field $\mathbb Z[\omega]/(\pi)$ has $p$ elements, and for $\alpha$ not divisible by $\pi$, $\alpha^{(p-1)/3}$ is congruent to one of $1, \omega, \omega^2$ modulo $\pi$. This defines the cubic residue symbol and leads to [[cubic-characters]] and cubic reciprocity, proved by Eisenstein in 1844 in this ring.
- $x^2 + xy + y^2$ is the reduced form of discriminant $-3$ in [[quadratic-forms]]; its class number is $1$, which is another way of saying $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ has unique factorization.
- The [[dedekind-zeta]] function of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ factors as $\zeta(s)L(s, \chi_{-3})$, and Hecke characters of this field give [[hecke-l]] functions. A 2026 manuscript (see [[quasi-rh]]) claims a zero-free half-plane for all Dirichlet $L$-functions using Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$; this is a claim, not an established result.
- Fermat's Last Theorem for exponent $3$ is naturally proved in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$; Kummer's work on other exponents needed [[ideals]] and [[cyclotomic]] fields.

1. Show that the six units of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ are pairwise incongruent modulo $3$.
2. Factor $91$ into primes of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and count the integer pairs $(a, b)$ with $a^2 - ab + b^2 = 91$.
3. Prove that if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ then the representation $p = x^2 + 3y^2$ with $x, y > 0$ is unique.
4. Show that $\mathbb Z[\omega]/(2)$ is a field with four elements.

blocks.body:
In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb Z\}$ the number $6$ factors in two genuinely different ways:
$$6 = 2\cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}),$$
and none of the four factors can be broken down further. Unique factorization, which carried the whole theory of [[gaussian-integers]], is simply false here.

The repair, found by Kummer and made precise by Dedekind, is to factor ideals instead of numbers. The four numbers above turn out to be products of four "ideal" prime factors, and the two factorizations of $6$ are two different ways of grouping the same four pieces. This lesson explains what that means and how to compute with it.

blocks.title: Where unique factorization breaks
blocks.body:
Give $\alpha = a + b\sqrt{-5}$ the norm $N(\alpha) = \alpha\bar\alpha = a^2 + 5b^2$, which is multiplicative. The units are $\pm 1$ (the only elements of norm $1$). The four factors above have norms
$$N(2) = 4, \quad N(3) = 9, \quad N(1 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 6.$$
If $2 = \beta\gamma$ with neither factor a unit, then $N(\beta) = 2$, i.e. $a^2 + 5b^2 = 2$, which is impossible. Likewise no element has norm $3$. So $2$, $3$ and $1 \pm\sqrt{-5}$ are all irreducible, and since the only units are $\pm 1$, no two of them are associates.

Something is missing: in a ring with unique factorization, $2$ would share a prime factor with $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ (because $2$ divides $(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$). That common factor would have norm $2$, and no such number exists. Kummer's insight was to add the missing common factors as new "ideal numbers"; Dedekind's was to realize them as sets of ordinary numbers.

blocks.title: Ring of integers
blocks.body:
A number field $K$ is a field containing $\mathbb Q$ of finite dimension over $\mathbb Q$. An algebraic integer is a complex number that is a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. The ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ is the set of algebraic integers in $K$; it is a ring, and $\mathcal O_K \cap \mathbb Q = \mathbb Z$.

For a quadratic field $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ with $d \ne 1$ squarefree,
$$\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\sqrt d] \ \text{ if } d \equiv 2, 3 \pmod 4, \qquad \mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z\Bigl[\tfrac{1 + \sqrt d}{2}\Bigr] \ \text{ if } d \equiv 1 \pmod 4.$$
So $\mathbb Z[i]$, $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ are the rings of integers of $\mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$. The ring of integers is the right place to do arithmetic: it is large enough that ideals factor uniquely.

blocks.title: Ideals, products and prime ideals
blocks.body:
In a commutative ring $R$ (see [[rings]]), an ideal is a nonempty subset $A$ closed under addition and under multiplication by arbitrary elements of $R$. The ideal generated by $a_1, \dots, a_k$ is $(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \{r_1a_1 + \dots + r_ka_k : r_j \in R\}$; an ideal $(a)$ with one generator is principal.

The product $AB$ of two ideals is the set of finite sums $\sum a_jb_j$ with $a_j \in A$, $b_j \in B$. In terms of generators, $(a_1, \dots, a_k)(b_1, \dots, b_m)$ is generated by all products $a_ib_j$; in particular $(a)(b) = (ab)$.

An ideal $P \ne R$ is prime if $ab \in P$ implies $a \in P$ or $b \in P$, equivalently if $R/P$ is an integral domain. In a ring of integers every nonzero prime ideal is maximal, so $\mathcal O_K/P$ is a finite field.

blocks.title: To contain is to divide
blocks.body:
For principal ideals, $(a) \supseteq (b)$ holds exactly when $b = ra$ for some $r$, that is when $a \mid b$; and $(a) = (b)$ exactly when $a$ and $b$ are associates. So factoring numbers up to units is the same as factoring principal ideals. The new feature is that there may be ideals that are not principal, and these play the role of Kummer's ideal numbers.

Here is the missing common factor of $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$. Let $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$. We claim
$$P_2 = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a \equiv b \pmod 2\}.$$
The map $a + b\sqrt{-5} \mapsto (a - b) \bmod 2$ is a ring homomorphism onto $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ (it sends $\sqrt{-5}$ to $1$, and $1^2 \equiv -5 \pmod 2$), so its kernel $Q = \{a \equiv b \pmod 2\}$ is an ideal with $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]/Q \cong \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. It contains $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, so $P_2 \subseteq Q$; conversely, if $a \equiv b \pmod 2$ then $a + b\sqrt{-5} = b(1 + \sqrt{-5}) + (a - b)$ with $a - b \in 2\mathbb Z$, so $Q \subseteq P_2$. Hence $P_2$ is a prime ideal of index $2$.

In exactly the same way, with $\sqrt{-5} \mapsto -1$ and $\sqrt{-5} \mapsto 1$ modulo $3$ (both square to $1 \equiv -5$),
$$P_3 = (3, 1 + \sqrt{-5}) = \{a \equiv b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)\}, \qquad P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5}) = \{a \equiv -b \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)\}$$
are prime ideals of index $3$.

None of these is principal. Multiplication by $\alpha = a + b\sqrt{-5}$ acts on the basis $1, \sqrt{-5}$ by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & -5b \\ b & a\end{pmatrix}$, so the index of $(\alpha)$ is the determinant $a^2 + 5b^2 = N(\alpha)$. A principal $P_2$ would need a generator of norm $2$, and a principal $P_3$ one of norm $3$; neither exists.

blocks.title: Dedekind's theorem (1871)
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a number field. Every nonzero ideal $A \ne \mathcal O_K$ is a product of prime ideals,
$$A = P_1^{e_1}\cdots P_r^{e_r},$$
and this factorization is unique apart from the order of the factors. Moreover $A \supseteq B$ if and only if $A \mid B$ (that is, $B = AC$ for some ideal $C$), and the norm $N(A) = |\mathcal O_K/A|$ is multiplicative, with $N((\alpha)) = |N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\alpha)|$.

blocks.title: About the proof
blocks.body:
The proof is omitted here; it takes a chapter in the books of Marcus or Neukirch listed below. The three properties of $\mathcal O_K$ that make it work are: every ideal is finitely generated; $\mathcal O_K$ is integrally closed (a fraction that is an algebraic integer already lies in $\mathcal O_K$); and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal. Rings with these properties are called Dedekind domains. The heart of the argument is that every nonzero ideal $A$ has an inverse: there is a fractional ideal $A^{-1}$ with $AA^{-1} = \mathcal O_K$. Cancellation of ideals then follows, and with it the "contain means divide" rule, from which existence and uniqueness of factorization follow much as for integers.

Integral closure is essential. In the smaller ring $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ the ideal $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-3})$ satisfies $(2, 1+\sqrt{-3})^2 = 2\,(2, 1+\sqrt{-3})$ although $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-3}) \ne (2)$, so ideals cannot be cancelled there.

blocks.title: Dedekind–Kummer factorization of primes
blocks.body:
Suppose $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\alpha]$ and $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. Let $p$ be a prime and factor $f$ modulo $p$ into distinct monic irreducibles, $f \equiv g_1^{e_1}\cdots g_r^{e_r} \pmod p$. Then
$$p\,\mathcal O_K = P_1^{e_1}\cdots P_r^{e_r}, \qquad P_j = (p, g_j(\alpha)), \qquad N(P_j) = p^{\deg g_j}.$$
(The proof is omitted; it follows from $\mathcal O_K/p\mathcal O_K \cong \mathbb F_p[x]/(\bar f)$.)

blocks.title: Primes in quadratic fields
blocks.body:
For $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ take $f = x^2 + 5$.

- Mod $2$: $x^2 + 5 \equiv (x + 1)^2$, so $(2) = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})^2 = P_2^2$. The prime $2$ ramifies.
- Mod $3$: $x^2 + 5 \equiv x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)$, so $(3) = (3, \sqrt{-5} - 1)(3, \sqrt{-5} + 1) = P_3'P_3$. The prime $3$ splits.
- Mod $7$: $3^2 = 9 \equiv -5$, so $x^2 + 5 \equiv (x - 3)(x + 3)$ and $(7) = P_7P_7'$ with $P_7 = (7, 3 + \sqrt{-5})$, $P_7' = (7, 3 - \sqrt{-5})$. Since $a^2 + 5b^2 = 7$ has no solutions, these are not principal either.
- Mod $11$: $-5 \equiv 6$ is not a square mod $11$ (the squares are $1, 3, 4, 5, 9$), so $x^2 + 5$ is irreducible and $(11)$ stays prime.

In general, for $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ and an odd prime $p \nmid d$, the prime $p$ splits into two distinct prime ideals when $\left(\frac dp\right) = 1$ and stays prime when $\left(\frac dp\right) = -1$; primes dividing the discriminant ramify. For $\mathbb Q(i)$ this is exactly the rule found for the Gaussian integers: $(p)$ splits when $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right) = 1$, i.e. $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

blocks.title: The two factorizations of 6
blocks.body:
Verify that in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$
$$(6) = (2, 1+\sqrt{-5})^2\,(3, 1+\sqrt{-5})(3, 1-\sqrt{-5}),$$
and explain both factorizations $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ in terms of these four prime ideals.
blocks.solution:
Write $s = \sqrt{-5}$, so $s^2 = -5$, and use the generator rule for products.

$P_2^2 = (4,\ 2(1+s),\ (1+s)^2) = (4,\ 2 + 2s,\ -4 + 2s)$. Every generator is divisible by $2$, so $P_2^2 \subseteq (2)$. Conversely $(2 + 2s) - (-4 + 2s) = 6$ and $6 - 4 = 2$ lie in $P_2^2$. So $P_2^2 = (2)$.

$P_3P_3' = (9,\ 3(1 - s),\ 3(1 + s),\ (1+s)(1-s)) = (9,\ 3 - 3s,\ 3 + 3s,\ 6)$. All generators are divisible by $3$, and $9 - 6 = 3$ is in the product. So $P_3P_3' = (3)$.

Multiplying, $(6) = (2)(3) = P_2^2P_3P_3'$.

Now regroup. $P_2P_3 = (6,\ 2(1+s),\ 3(1+s),\ (1+s)^2)$. Each generator is a multiple of $1 + s$ (note $6 = (1+s)(1-s)$), and $3(1+s) - 2(1+s) = 1 + s$ is in the product, so $P_2P_3 = (1 + s)$. By conjugation, $P_2P_3' = (1 - s)$.

So the two factorizations of the number $6$ are
$$(2)(3) = (P_2P_2)(P_3P_3'), \qquad (1 + s)(1 - s) = (P_2P_3)(P_2P_3').$$
The same four prime ideals appear, grouped in two ways. Neither $2$ nor $1+s$ is prime as an element because each is a product of two non-principal prime ideals. As a check on norms: $N(P_2)^2N(P_3)N(P_3') = 4 \cdot 9 = 36 = N(6)$.

blocks.title: Factoring a principal ideal
blocks.body: Factor the ideal $(3 + \sqrt{-5})$ into prime ideals.
blocks.solution:
$N(3 + \sqrt{-5}) = 9 + 5 = 14 = 2\cdot 7$, so by multiplicativity of the norm $(3 + \sqrt{-5})$ is a product of a prime ideal of norm $2$ and one of norm $7$. The only prime of norm $2$ is $P_2$, which contains $3 + \sqrt{-5}$ (since $3 \equiv 1 \pmod 2$). The primes of norm $7$ are $P_7 = (7, 3 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $P_7' = (7, 3 - \sqrt{-5})$. Clearly $3 + \sqrt{-5} \in P_7$. It is not in $P_7'$: otherwise $P_7'$ would contain $(3 + \sqrt{-5}) + (3 - \sqrt{-5}) = 6$ and $7$, hence $1$.

Since containing means dividing, $P_2 \mid (3 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $P_7 \mid (3 + \sqrt{-5})$, so
$$(3 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2\,P_7.$$
Similarly $(3 - \sqrt{-5}) = P_2P_7'$, and $14 = (3 + \sqrt{-5})(3 - \sqrt{-5})$ corresponds to $(2)(7) = P_2^2P_7P_7'$.

blocks.title: A gcd that is not a number
blocks.body: Show that in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the only common divisors of $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ are $\pm 1$, yet there are no $x, y \in \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ with $2x + (1+\sqrt{-5})y = 1$.
blocks.solution:
If $\delta$ divides both, then $N(\delta)$ divides $N(2) = 4$ and $N(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = 6$, so $N(\delta) \in \{1, 2\}$. No element has norm $2$, so $N(\delta) = 1$ and $\delta = \pm 1$.

Now write $x = a + b\sqrt{-5}$ and $y = c + e\sqrt{-5}$ with integers $a, b, c, e$. Then
$$2x + (1 + \sqrt{-5})y = (2a + c - 5e) + (2b + c + e)\sqrt{-5}.$$
For this to equal $1$ we need $2a + c - 5e = 1$ and $2b + c + e = 0$. Subtracting, $2a - 2b - 6e = 1$, whose left side is even. Contradiction.

In $\mathbb Z$ (and in $\mathbb Z[i]$), coprime numbers always satisfy such a Bézout relation. Here they do not, because the set of all combinations $2x + (1 + \sqrt{-5})y$ is the ideal $P_2$, which is neither the whole ring nor generated by a single number. The ideal $P_2$ is the honest greatest common divisor of $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$.

blocks.title: Kummer, Dedekind and Fermat
blocks.body:
The ideas grew out of Fermat's Last Theorem. For an odd prime $p$ and $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/p}$, the equation $x^p + y^p = z^p$ factors as
$$\prod_{k=0}^{p-1}(x + \zeta^k y) = z^p$$
in $\mathbb Z[\zeta]$. With unique factorization one could argue as in the Gaussian example $x^2 + 1 = y^3$: coprime factors whose product is a $p$-th power are $p$-th powers up to units. But unique factorization in $\mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$ fails for many $p$, the first being $p = 23$.

In 1847 Kummer introduced his ideal numbers, restoring unique factorization in these cyclotomic rings, and proved Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes, those $p$ that do not divide the class number of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$. In 1871 Dedekind replaced ideal numbers by ideals, sets of actual numbers, and proved unique factorization of ideals in every ring of integers. The extent to which ideals fail to be principal is measured by the [[class-group]].

- Irreducible is not the same as prime. In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the element $2$ is irreducible but not prime: it divides $(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ and neither factor.
- An ideal with two generators is not "a pair of numbers"; different generator sets can give the same ideal, e.g. $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-5}) = (2, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$ since $1 - \sqrt{-5} = 2 - (1 + \sqrt{-5})$.
- The Dedekind–Kummer recipe requires $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\alpha]$ (or at least $p \nmid [\mathcal O_K : \mathbb Z[\alpha]]$). Applied to $x^2 + 3$ and $p = 2$ it would give the wrong answer for $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, where $2$ is actually inert.

- The quotient of all (fractional) ideals by the principal ones is the [[class-group]]; it is trivial exactly when $\mathcal O_K$ has unique factorization of elements.
- In [[cyclotomic]] fields, the Dedekind–Kummer theorem applied to the cyclotomic polynomial shows that a prime $p \nmid n$ splits in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ according to the order of $p$ modulo $n$.
- Summing $N(A)^{-s}$ over all nonzero ideals gives the [[dedekind-zeta]] function; unique factorization of ideals is exactly what gives it an Euler product over prime ideals.
- Ideal classes and characters on ideals lead on to [[hecke-l]] functions.
- The [[gaussian-integers]] and [[eisenstein-integers]] are the cases where every ideal is principal, so ideal factorization and element factorization agree.

1. Show that $(2, 1+\sqrt{-5})(3, 1-\sqrt{-5}) = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$.
2. Use the Dedekind–Kummer theorem to factor $(29)$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, and decide whether its prime factors are principal.
3. Show that $(7, 3 + \sqrt{-5})^2$ is principal by finding a generator. (Hint: look for an element of norm $49$ other than $\pm 7$.)
4. Factor $(2)$ and $(3)$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-6}]$ and show that the prime ideals above $2$ and $3$ are not principal.

Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory
Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory

blocks.body:
In a ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$, ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals (see [[ideals]]), but numbers may not. The two statements agree exactly when every ideal is principal. So the natural measure of how badly unique factorization fails is: how many ideals are not principal, and in how many essentially different ways?

The answer is a finite abelian group, the ideal class group, and its order is the class number $h_K$. Class numbers connect algebra (unique factorization), Gauss's theory of [[quadratic-forms]], analysis (values of $L$-functions) and some famous numerical coincidences, such as $e^{\pi\sqrt{163}}$ being within $10^{-12}$ of an integer.

blocks.title: Class group and class number
blocks.body:
A fractional ideal of $K$ is a set of the form $\tfrac1d A$ with $A$ a nonzero ideal of $\mathcal O_K$ and $d$ a nonzero integer. By Dedekind's theory the fractional ideals form an abelian group $I_K$ under multiplication, with identity $\mathcal O_K$; the inverse of $A$ is $A^{-1} = \{x \in K : xA \subseteq \mathcal O_K\}$. The principal fractional ideals $\alpha\mathcal O_K$, $\alpha \in K^\times$, form a subgroup $P_K$. The class group and class number are
$$\mathrm{Cl}(K) = I_K/P_K, \qquad h_K = |\mathrm{Cl}(K)|.$$

Concretely, two nonzero ideals $A, B$ of $\mathcal O_K$ are in the same class exactly when $(\alpha)A = (\beta)B$ for some nonzero $\alpha, \beta \in \mathcal O_K$. The trivial class consists of the principal ideals.

blocks.title: Class number one means unique factorization
blocks.body: $h_K = 1$ if and only if $\mathcal O_K$ has unique factorization of elements into primes (up to order and units).

Suppose $h_K = 1$, so every ideal is principal. Every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles, by induction on $|N(\alpha)|$. If $\pi$ is irreducible, $(\pi)$ lies in some maximal ideal $P = (\rho)$; then $\rho \mid \pi$ and $\rho$ is not a unit, so $\rho$ is an associate of $\pi$ and $(\pi) = P$ is a prime ideal. Thus irreducibles are prime ($\pi \mid \alpha\beta$ implies $\pi \mid \alpha$ or $\pi \mid \beta$), and uniqueness follows as in $\mathbb Z$.

Conversely, suppose $\mathcal O_K$ has unique factorization, and let $P$ be a nonzero prime ideal. Pick a nonzero $\alpha \in P$ and factor it into primes, $\alpha = \pi_1\cdots\pi_r$. As $P$ is a prime ideal, some $\pi_j$ lies in $P$. Since $\pi_j$ is a prime element, $(\pi_j)$ is a nonzero prime ideal, hence maximal, and $(\pi_j) \subseteq P \ne \mathcal O_K$ forces $(\pi_j) = P$. So every prime ideal is principal, and since every nonzero ideal is a product of prime ideals, every ideal is principal.

blocks.title: Finiteness of the class group (Minkowski bound)
blocks.body:
Let $K$ have degree $n$, discriminant $d_K$, and $r_2$ pairs of complex embeddings. Every ideal class contains an ideal $A \subseteq \mathcal O_K$ with
$$N(A) \le M_K = \frac{n!}{n^n}\Bigl(\frac4\pi\Bigr)^{r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}.$$
For an imaginary quadratic field $M_K = \tfrac2\pi\sqrt{|d_K|}$; for a real quadratic field $M_K = \tfrac12\sqrt{d_K}$. Since an ideal of norm $m$ contains $m$, and $\mathcal O_K/(m)$ is finite, only finitely many ideals have norm at most $M_K$; hence $h_K$ is finite.

blocks.title: About the proof, and a practical recipe
blocks.body:
The bound comes from Minkowski's geometry of numbers: a symmetric convex region of large enough volume contains a nonzero lattice point, and applied to the lattice $A^{-1}$ this produces an element of controlled norm. The proof is omitted here (see Marcus, Ch. 5).

The recipe it gives: list the prime ideals of norm at most $M_K$ (they lie above rational primes $p \le M_K$ and are found by the Dedekind–Kummer theorem), decide which products of them are principal, and read off the group. For $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$, $d_K = -20$ and $M_K = \tfrac2\pi\sqrt{20} \approx 2.85$. The only ideals of norm $\le 2$ are $\mathcal O_K$ and $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, and $P_2$ is not principal because $a^2 + 5b^2 = 2$ has no solution. So $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5}))$ has order $2$, generated by the class of $P_2$, and indeed $P_2^2 = (2)$.

For $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-7})$ ($d_K = -7$) the bound is $\tfrac2\pi\sqrt 7 \approx 1.68$, so every class contains $\mathcal O_K$ and $h = 1$ with no further work.

blocks.title: Ideals and binary quadratic forms
blocks.body:
For imaginary quadratic fields Gauss's older theory gives an efficient way to compute. Let $D = d_K < 0$. If an ideal $A$ has $\mathbb Z$-basis $\alpha, \beta$ (suitably oriented), then
$$f_A(x, y) = \frac{N(x\alpha + y\beta)}{N(A)}$$
is a primitive positive definite form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with integer coefficients and $b^2 - 4ac = D$; for instance $A = \mathbb Z a + \mathbb Z\,\tfrac{-b + \sqrt D}{2}$ gives back $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$. This sets up a bijection between $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ and proper equivalence classes of such forms, under which ideal multiplication becomes Gauss composition. (Proof omitted; see Cox's book.)

Each class of forms contains exactly one reduced form: $|b| \le a \le c$, with $b \ge 0$ if $|b| = a$ or $a = c$. For a reduced form $|D| = 4ac - b^2 \ge 4a^2 - a^2 = 3a^2$, so $a \le \sqrt{|D|/3}$, and counting reduced forms is a finite search. This is how the class numbers in this lesson are computed. Write $h(D)$ for the class number of the field of discriminant $D$.

blocks.title: h(−20) = 2 and the primes x² + 5y²
blocks.body: Compute $h(-20)$ by reduced forms, and explain which primes are of the form $x^2 + 5y^2$.
blocks.solution:
We need $b^2 - 4ac = -20$, so $b$ is even, and $a \le \sqrt{20/3} \approx 2.58$.

- $a = 1$: $b = 0$ (since $|b| \le 1$ and $b$ even), $c = 5$: the form $x^2 + 5y^2$.
- $a = 2$: $b = 0$ gives $8c = 20$, no; $b = \pm 2$ gives $4 - 8c = -20$, $c = 3$; as $|b| = a$ we keep only $b = 2$: the form $2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$.

So $h(-20) = 2$, agreeing with the Minkowski computation. The non-principal form comes from $P_2 = \mathbb Z\cdot 2 + \mathbb Z(1 + \sqrt{-5})$:
$$\frac{N(2x + (1+\sqrt{-5})y)}{2} = \frac{(2x+y)^2 + 5y^2}{2} = 2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2.$$

For a prime $p \ne 2, 5$: $p$ splits in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ iff $\left(\frac{-5}{p}\right) = 1$, which happens iff $p \equiv 1, 3, 7, 9 \pmod{20}$. If $p = PP'$ with $P$ principal, $P = (x + y\sqrt{-5})$ and $p = x^2 + 5y^2$; if $P$ is not principal, $p$ is represented by $2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2$ instead. Which case occurs is decided by $p$ modulo $20$ (this is genus theory):
$$p = x^2 + 5y^2 \iff p \equiv 1, 9 \pmod{20}, \qquad p = 2x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2 \iff p \equiv 3, 7 \pmod{20}.$$
For example $29 \equiv 9 \pmod{20}$ and $29 = 3^2 + 5\cdot 2^2$, while $3 = 2\cdot 0^2 + 2\cdot 0\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 1^2$ and $7 = 2\cdot 1^2 + 2\cdot 1\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 1^2$ are represented by the second form and not by $x^2 + 5y^2$.

blocks.title: A class group of order 3
blocks.body: Let $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-23})$, with $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\theta]$, $\theta = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-23}}{2}$. Show that $h(-23) = 3$ and that a prime ideal above $2$ has order $3$ in the class group.
blocks.solution:
Reduced forms of discriminant $-23$: $b$ is odd and $a \le \sqrt{23/3} \approx 2.77$. For $a = 1$, $b = 1$, $c = 6$. For $a = 2$, $b = \pm 1$, $c = 3$, and both signs are allowed since $|b| < a < c$. So the reduced forms are $x^2 + xy + 6y^2$ and $2x^2 \pm xy + 3y^2$, and $h(-23) = 3$; a group of order $3$ is cyclic.

Directly: $\theta$ has minimal polynomial $x^2 - x + 6$, and $N(x + y\theta) = x^2 + xy + 6y^2$, so $4N(x + y\theta) = (2x + y)^2 + 23y^2$. Modulo $2$, $x^2 - x + 6 \equiv x(x - 1)$, so $(2) = PP'$ with $P = (2, \theta)$, $P' = (2, \theta - 1)$, each of norm $2$. $P$ is not principal: an element of norm $2$ would need $y = 0$ (else $4N \ge 23$) and then $x^2 = 2$.

Now $N(1 + \theta) = 1 + 1 + 6 = 8$, so $(1 + \theta)$ is a product of three prime ideals of norm $2$, i.e. $P^aP'^b$ with $a + b = 3$. If both $a, b \ge 1$, then $PP' = (2)$ would divide $(1 + \theta)$, i.e. $2 \mid 1 + \theta = \tfrac{3 + \sqrt{-23}}{2}$, which is false since $\tfrac{3 + \sqrt{-23}}{4} \notin \mathcal O_K$. So $(1 + \theta) = P^3$ or $P'^3$, and since $P' = P^{-1}$ up to the principal ideal $(2)$, in either case $P^3$ is principal while $P$ is not. The class of $P$ has order $3$.

blocks.title: Euler's prime-producing polynomial
blocks.body: Using $h(-163) = 1$, show that $n^2 + n + 41$ is prime for $n = 0, 1, \dots, 39$.
blocks.solution:
Let $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-163})$, $\theta = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-163}}{2}$, so $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\theta]$ and $\theta$ has minimal polynomial $x^2 - x + 41$ (indeed $\theta + \bar\theta = 1$ and $\theta\bar\theta = \tfrac{1 + 163}{4} = 41$). Then
$$N(x + y\theta) = x^2 + xy + 41y^2, \qquad 4N(x + y\theta) = (2x + y)^2 + 163y^2.$$

For $0 \le n \le 39$ we have $n^2 + n + 41 \le 1601 < 41^2$, so it is enough to show that no prime $p < 41$ divides $n^2 + n + 41$. Suppose one did. Since $n^2 + n$ is even, $n^2 + n + 41$ is odd and $p$ is odd. The polynomial $x^2 - x + 41$ has the root $-n$ modulo $p$, so by the Dedekind–Kummer theorem $p$ is not inert: there is a prime ideal $P$ of norm $p$. As $h = 1$, $P = (x + y\theta)$ and $x^2 + xy + 41y^2 = p$. If $y = 0$ then $p = x^2$, impossible; if $y \ne 0$ then $4p \ge 163$, so $p \ge 41$. Contradiction.

At $n = 40$ the pattern stops: $40^2 + 40 + 41 = 41^2$. The same argument shows that $n^2 + n + A$ is prime for $0 \le n \le A - 2$ whenever $1 - 4A$ is one of the discriminants of class number one, giving $A = 2, 3, 5, 11, 17, 41$ (Rabinowitsch's criterion; the converse also holds).

blocks.title: Class number one (Heegner, Baker, Stark)
blocks.body:
For squarefree $d > 0$, the field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})$ has class number $1$ exactly for
$$d = 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163,$$
equivalently for the discriminants $D = -3, -4, -7, -8, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163$.

blocks.title: History, and the near-integer
blocks.body:
Gauss, in the language of forms, conjectured that his list of discriminants of class number one was complete. Heegner gave a proof in 1952 using modular functions; it was initially doubted and later accepted. Baker (1966) and Stark (1967) gave independent proofs by quite different methods.

The near-integer comes from the modular $j$-function, $j(\tau) = q^{-1} + 744 + 196884q + \cdots$ with $q = e^{2\pi i\tau}$. A deep fact of the theory of complex multiplication is that $j\bigl(\tfrac{1 + \sqrt D}{2}\bigr)$, for odd $D$, is an algebraic integer of degree $h(D)$. When $h = 1$ it is an ordinary integer; for $D = -163$ it is $-640320^3$. Here $q = e^{\pi i}e^{-\pi\sqrt{163}} = -e^{-\pi\sqrt{163}}$, so
$$e^{\pi\sqrt{163}} = 640320^3 + 744 - 196884\,e^{-\pi\sqrt{163}} + \cdots \approx 640320^3 + 744 - 7.5\times 10^{-13}.$$
The same happens, less spectacularly, for $67$ and $43$: $e^{\pi\sqrt{67}} \approx 5280^3 + 744$ and $e^{\pi\sqrt{43}} \approx 960^3 + 744$. The number $e^{\pi\sqrt{163}}$ is not an integer; by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem it is transcendental.

blocks.title: How fast do class numbers grow?
blocks.body:
For imaginary quadratic fields, Dirichlet's class number formula links $h$ to a value of an $L$-function (see [[class-number-formula]]):
$$h(D) = \frac{w\sqrt{|D|}}{2\pi}L(1, \chi_D),$$
where $\chi_D$ is the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac Dn\right)$ and $w$ is the number of roots of unity in $K$ ($w = 6$ for $D = -3$, $w = 4$ for $D = -4$, $w = 2$ otherwise). For $D < -4$ it can be rewritten as a finite sum, $h(D) = -\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{a=1}^{|D|-1}\chi_D(a)\,a$.

Since $L(1, \chi_D) \ll \log|D|$, one gets $h(D) \ll \sqrt{|D|}\log|D|$. In the other direction, Siegel proved in 1935 that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $c(\varepsilon) > 0$ with $h(D) > c(\varepsilon)|D|^{1/2 - \varepsilon}$, so $h(D) \to \infty$. But $c(\varepsilon)$ cannot be computed from the proof: it could only be small if $L(s, \chi_D)$ had a real zero very close to $s = 1$, a Siegel zero, and the argument cannot rule such a zero out effectively. This is why class numbers and [[siegel-zeros]] are tied together. The effective lower bounds known today, from work of Goldfeld and of Gross and Zagier, grow only roughly like $\log|D|$.

For real quadratic fields the situation is reversed: class numbers are often $1$, and Gauss's conjecture that infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number $1$ is still open.

- $h(-163)$ refers to the discriminant $D = -163$, the field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-163})$. For $d \equiv 1, 2 \pmod 4$ the discriminant is $-4d$, not $-d$: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ has $D = -20$.
- The list of nine is for imaginary quadratic fields. Many real quadratic fields have class number $1$ (for instance $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 5)$), and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{10})$ has class number $2$.
- Class number $1$ does not mean the ring is Euclidean: $\mathbb Z\bigl[\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-19}}{2}\bigr]$ has unique factorization but no division algorithm with respect to any function.
- Class numbers of forms of non-fundamental discriminant (for example $x^2 + 3y^2$, discriminant $-12$) belong to orders like $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$, not to the full ring of integers; do not mix the two.

- The general analytic class number formula expresses $h_K$ through the residue of the [[dedekind-zeta]] function at $s = 1$; see [[class-number-formula]].
- The ineffectivity in Siegel's bound is the same phenomenon as possible [[siegel-zeros]]; ruling them out (see [[no-siegel]]) would make the bound effective.
- Characters of the class group are the simplest Hecke characters, and their $L$-functions are [[hecke-l]] functions; the trivial character gives back $\zeta_K(s)$.
- Kummer's regular primes are those $p$ not dividing the class number of the [[cyclotomic]] field $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$.
- Reduced forms and Gauss composition are developed in [[quadratic-forms]].

blocks.body:
The $n$-th roots of unity $1, \zeta_n, \zeta_n^2, \dots, \zeta_n^{n-1}$, with $\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$, are the corners of a regular $n$-gon. Adjoining them to $\mathbb Q$ gives the cyclotomic field $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ ("circle-dividing"). These fields are where Gauss found his ruler-and-compass construction of the regular $17$-gon, where Kummer attacked Fermat's Last Theorem, and, by the Kronecker–Weber theorem, they contain every abelian extension of $\mathbb Q$.

Two facts organize everything: $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ has degree $\varphi(n)$, and a prime $p \nmid n$ factors in it according to the order of $p$ modulo $n$. This lesson proves both.

blocks.title: Cyclotomic polynomial
blocks.body:
A primitive $n$-th root of unity is a complex number of multiplicative order exactly $n$; these are $\zeta_n^k$ with $1 \le k \le n$ and $\gcd(k, n) = 1$. The $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial is
$$\Phi_n(x) = \prod_{\substack{1 \le k \le n \\ \gcd(k,n)=1}} \bigl(x - e^{2\pi i k/n}\bigr),$$
a monic polynomial of degree $\varphi(n)$. Its roots are exactly the primitive $n$-th roots of unity.

blocks.title: First properties
blocks.body:
Every $n$-th root of unity is a primitive $d$-th root of unity for exactly one divisor $d$ of $n$ (its order). Grouping the roots of $x^n - 1$ by order gives
$$x^n - 1 = \prod_{d \mid n}\Phi_d(x).$$
This lets us compute $\Phi_n$ recursively by polynomial division, and since we keep dividing monic integer polynomials by monic integer polynomials, every $\Phi_n$ has integer coefficients. The first few:
$$\Phi_1 = x - 1,\quad \Phi_2 = x + 1,\quad \Phi_3 = x^2 + x + 1,\quad \Phi_4 = x^2 + 1,\quad \Phi_6 = x^2 - x + 1,\quad \Phi_{12} = x^4 - x^2 + 1,$$
and for a prime $p$, $\Phi_p = (x^p - 1)/(x - 1) = x^{p-1} + \dots + x + 1$.

Comparing degrees in the product formula gives the identity $\sum_{d \mid n}\varphi(d) = n$. Also $\Phi_n(0) = 1$ for $n \ge 2$, and $\Phi_p(1) = p$.

The cyclotomic field $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ is the smallest field containing $\zeta_n$; its elements are polynomials in $\zeta_n$ with rational coefficients. Its ring of integers is $\mathbb Z[\zeta_n]$ (a standard fact, which we use without proof).

blocks.title: Irreducibility of Φₙ
blocks.body:
$\Phi_n(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. Consequently
$$[\mathbb Q(\zeta_n):\mathbb Q] = \varphi(n).$$

Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\zeta = \zeta_n$ over $\mathbb Q$. Since $f$ is monic and divides $x^n - 1$, Gauss's lemma gives $f \in \mathbb Z[x]$; write $x^n - 1 = f(x)g(x)$ with $g \in \mathbb Z[x]$ monic.

Claim: if $\eta$ is a root of $f$ and $p$ is a prime not dividing $n$, then $\eta^p$ is also a root of $f$. Suppose not. Since $\eta^p$ is an $n$-th root of unity, $g(\eta^p) = 0$, so $\eta$ is a root of $g(x^p)$, and as $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\eta$, $f(x) \mid g(x^p)$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$. Reduce modulo $p$ and write bars for reductions. In $\mathbb F_p[x]$ we have $\bar g(x^p) = \bar g(x)^p$, because $(a + b)^p = a^p + b^p$ in characteristic $p$ and $c^p = c$ for $c \in \mathbb F_p$. So $\bar f \mid \bar g^{\,p}$, and some irreducible $\bar h$ divides both $\bar f$ and $\bar g$. Then $\bar h^2$ divides $\bar f\bar g = x^n - 1$ in $\mathbb F_p[x]$. But $x^n - 1$ has no repeated factor modulo $p$: its derivative $nx^{n-1}$ is nonzero (as $p \nmid n$) and has only the root $0$, which is not a root of $x^n - 1$. Contradiction.

Now any primitive root $\zeta^k$, $\gcd(k, n) = 1$, is reached from $\zeta$ by raising to primes not dividing $n$ one at a time (factor $k = p_1p_2\cdots p_r$). By the claim each step stays among the roots of $f$. So all $\varphi(n)$ primitive roots are roots of $f$, $\deg f \ge \varphi(n) = \deg\Phi_n$, and since $f \mid \Phi_n$ we get $f = \Phi_n$.

blocks.title: The Galois group
blocks.body:
Because the conjugates of $\zeta_n$ are its powers $\zeta_n^a$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, each such $a$ gives a field automorphism $\sigma_a$ of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ with $\sigma_a(\zeta_n) = \zeta_n^a$, and $\sigma_a\sigma_b = \sigma_{ab}$. So
$$\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)/\mathbb Q) \cong (\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times,$$
an abelian group (see [[galois]]). The automorphism $\sigma_p$ attached to a prime $p \nmid n$ is the Frobenius element at $p$, and its order, which is the order of $p$ modulo $n$, controls how $p$ factors.

blocks.title: Splitting of primes in Q(ζₙ)
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \nmid n$, and let $f$ be the order of $p$ modulo $n$ (see [[order-primroot]]). Then
$$p\,\mathbb Z[\zeta_n] = P_1P_2\cdots P_g, \qquad g = \frac{\varphi(n)}{f},$$
with distinct prime ideals $P_j$, each of norm $N(P_j) = p^f$. In particular $p$ splits completely (into $\varphi(n)$ primes of norm $p$) if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Primes dividing $n$ ramify; for instance $p\,\mathbb Z[\zeta_p] = (1 - \zeta_p)^{p-1}$.

By the Dedekind–Kummer theorem (see [[ideals]]), applied to $\mathcal O = \mathbb Z[\zeta_n]$ and $\Phi_n$, it suffices to show that $\Phi_n$ modulo $p$ is a product of distinct irreducible factors, each of degree $f$. Distinctness holds because $\Phi_n$ divides $x^n - 1$, which has no repeated factors modulo $p$ (shown in the previous proof).

Let $\bar h$ be an irreducible factor of $\Phi_n$ modulo $p$, of degree $k$. Then $F = \mathbb F_p[x]/(\bar h)$ is a field with $p^k$ elements, and the class $\beta$ of $x$ is a root of $\Phi_n$ that generates $F$. Its order in $F^\times$ is exactly $n$: certainly $\beta^n = 1$, and if $\beta^d = 1$ for a proper divisor $d$ of $n$, then $\beta$ would be a root of some $\Phi_e$ with $e \mid d$ as well as of $\Phi_n$, hence a repeated root of $x^n - 1 = \prod_{e \mid n}\Phi_e$, which is impossible.

Since $F^\times$ has order $p^k - 1$, we get $n \mid p^k - 1$, so $k \ge f$. Conversely, $n \mid p^f - 1$ gives $\beta^{p^f} = \beta$. The roots of $x^{p^f} - x$ in $F$ form a subfield (because $(a+b)^{p^f} = a^{p^f} + b^{p^f}$) with at most $p^f$ elements, and it contains the generator $\beta$, so it is all of $F$ and $p^k \le p^f$. Hence $k = f$, and $\Phi_n$ splits modulo $p$ into $\varphi(n)/f$ distinct factors of degree $f$.

For the ramified example: $p = \Phi_p(1) = \prod_{k=1}^{p-1}(1 - \zeta_p^k)$, and each quotient $(1 - \zeta_p^k)/(1 - \zeta_p) = 1 + \zeta_p + \dots + \zeta_p^{k-1}$ is a unit: choosing $m$ with $km \equiv 1 \pmod p$, its inverse is $(1 - \zeta_p)/(1 - \zeta_p^k) = 1 + \zeta_p^k + \zeta_p^{2k} + \dots + \zeta_p^{(m-1)k}$, also in $\mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$. So $(p) = (1 - \zeta_p)^{p-1}$, and comparing norms, $(1 - \zeta_p)$ is a prime ideal of norm $p$.

blocks.title: Primes in Q(ζ₁₂)
blocks.body: Describe how the primes $5, 7, 11, 13$ factor in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})$, and check it against the factorization of $\Phi_{12} = x^4 - x^2 + 1$ modulo these primes.
blocks.solution:
Here $\varphi(12) = 4$. The group $(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z)^\times = \{1, 5, 7, 11\}$ has every element of order at most $2$: $5^2 = 25$, $7^2 = 49$ and $11^2 = 121$ are all $\equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

- $p = 13 \equiv 1$: $f = 1$, so $13$ splits into $4$ primes of norm $13$. Indeed $x^4 - x^2 + 1 \equiv (x - 2)(x + 2)(x - 6)(x + 6) \pmod{13}$; for example $2^4 - 2^2 + 1 = 13$.
- $p = 5, 7, 11$: $f = 2$, so each splits into $2$ primes of norm $p^2$. Modulo $5$: $(x^2 + 2x - 1)(x^2 - 2x - 1)$. Modulo $7$: $(x^2 + 2)(x^2 - 3)$. Modulo $11$: $(x^2 + 5x + 1)(x^2 - 5x + 1)$.

The field is $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12}) = \mathbb Q(i, \sqrt 3)$, since $\zeta_{12} = \tfrac{\sqrt 3 + i}{2}$. Each $p \ne 2, 3$ splits in exactly one or all three of the quadratic subfields $\mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 3)$, which is another way to see why it can never stay prime in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})$.

blocks.title: Gauss and the regular 17-gon
blocks.body:
Let $\zeta = \zeta_{17}$. Split the sixteen primitive roots into two sums of eight,
$$\eta_0 = \sum_{r \in R}\zeta^r, \qquad \eta_1 = \sum_{r \in N}\zeta^r,$$
where $R = \{1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 13, 15, 16\}$ is the set of nonzero squares modulo $17$ and $N$ its complement. Show that $\eta_0, \eta_1$ are the roots of $x^2 + x - 4$, and explain why the $17$-gon is constructible.
blocks.solution:
First, $\eta_0 + \eta_1 = \sum_{k=1}^{16}\zeta^k = \Phi_{17}(\zeta) - 1 = -1$.

Second, since $-1 \equiv 16$ is a square modulo $17$, the set $R$ is closed under $r \mapsto -r$, so $\eta_0 = 2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{17} + \cos\tfrac{4\pi}{17} + \cos\tfrac{8\pi}{17} + \cos\tfrac{16\pi}{17}\bigr) \approx 1.5616$ is real, and similarly $\eta_1 \approx -2.5616$. The product $\eta_0\eta_1$ is a sum of $64$ terms $\zeta^{r+s}$, $r \in R$, $s \in N$. None of them is $\zeta^0$, because $r + s \equiv 0$ would put $s = -r$ in $R$. Multiplying all $64$ exponents by a nonzero residue $a$ permutes this multiset of exponents: a square $a$ maps $R$ to $R$ and $N$ to $N$, a non-square swaps them, and either way the pairs $(r, s)$ are permuted. Since multiplication by suitable $a$ carries any nonzero residue to any other, each of the $16$ nonzero residues occurs equally often, four times. Hence $\eta_0\eta_1 = 4\sum_{k=1}^{16}\zeta^k = -4$.

So $\eta_0, \eta_1$ are the roots of $x^2 + x - 4$, namely $\tfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}$, with $\eta_0 = \tfrac{-1 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$.

The Galois group $(\mathbb Z/17\mathbb Z)^\times$ is cyclic of order $16 = 2^4$ (generated by $3$). Repeating the idea, the eight-term sums split into four-term sums that satisfy quadratics over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{17})$, and those into two-term sums such as $\zeta + \zeta^{-1} = 2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{17}$, which is therefore reached after three quadratic steps (a fourth gives $\zeta$ itself). Square roots can be constructed with ruler and compass, so $\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{17}$ and the $17$-gon are constructible; Gauss found this in 1796. In general the regular $n$-gon is constructible exactly when $\varphi(n)$ is a power of $2$ (Gauss and Wantzel).

blocks.title: Infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod n)
blocks.body: Let $n \ge 2$. Show that if a prime $q \nmid n$ divides $\Phi_n(a)$ for an integer $a$, then $q \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Deduce that there are infinitely many primes $q \equiv 1 \pmod n$.
blocks.solution:
Since $\Phi_n(a) \mid a^n - 1$, we have $a^n \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so $q 
mid a$ and the order $d$ of $a$ modulo $q$ divides $n$. If $d < n$, then $a$ is a root modulo $q$ of $x^d - 1 = \prod_{e \mid d}\Phi_e(x)$, hence of some $\Phi_e$ with $e < n$, $e \mid n$, as well as of $\Phi_n$. Then $a$ would be a repeated root of $x^n - 1$ modulo $q$, impossible since $q 
mid n$. So $d = n$, and by Fermat's little theorem $n \mid q - 1$.

Now suppose $p_1, \dots, p_k$ were all the primes $\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Put $a = t\,n\,p_1\cdots p_k$ with $t$ a positive integer large enough that $\Phi_n(a) > 1$ (possible since $\Phi_n$ is monic of positive degree). As $\Phi_n$ has integer coefficients, $\Phi_n(a) \equiv \Phi_n(0) = 1 \pmod a$. Let $q$ be a prime factor of $\Phi_n(a)$. Then $q 
mid a$, so $q 
mid n$ and $q 
e p_j$; but by the first part $q \equiv 1 \pmod n$, a contradiction.

Illustration: $\Phi_5(5) = 625 + 125 + 25 + 5 + 1 = 781 = 11 \cdot 71$, and both $11$ and $71$ are $\equiv 1 \pmod 5$.

blocks.title: Kummer, regular primes, and Kronecker–Weber
blocks.body:
For an odd prime $p$, Fermat's equation $x^p + y^p = z^p$ becomes $\prod_{k=0}^{p-1}(x + \zeta_p^ky) = z^p$ in $\mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$. The ring $\mathbb Z[\zeta_p]$ has unique factorization only for $p \le 19$; for $p = 23$ its class number is $3$. In 1847 Kummer introduced ideal numbers to handle this and proved Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes, those $p$ not dividing the class number of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$. He also gave a practical test: $p$ is regular if and only if $p$ divides none of the numerators of the Bernoulli numbers $B_2, B_4, \dots, B_{p-3}$. The smallest irregular prime is $37$, which divides the numerator of $B_{32}$.

Every quadratic field sits inside a cyclotomic field. For an odd prime $p$, the quadratic Gauss sum $g = \sum_{t=1}^{p-1}\left(\frac tp\right)\zeta_p^t$ satisfies $g^2 = \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)p$ (see [[gauss-sums]]), so $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{\pm p}) \subseteq \mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$, with the sign making $\pm p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. For example $\zeta_5 - \zeta_5^2 - \zeta_5^3 + \zeta_5^4 = \sqrt 5$.

The Kronecker–Weber theorem says much more: every finite Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$ with abelian Galois group is contained in some $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$. (Proof omitted; it is a cornerstone of class field theory.)

- The splitting is governed by the order of $p$ modulo $n$, not by anything modulo $p$. For $n = 12$ and $p = 5$, $f = 2$ because $5^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.
- Coefficients of $\Phi_n$ are not always $0$ or $\pm 1$. The first exception is $\Phi_{105}$, which has a coefficient $-2$.
- For odd $n$, $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n) = \mathbb Q(\zeta_{2n})$ because $-\zeta_n$ is a primitive $2n$-th root of unity; consistently, $\varphi(2n) = \varphi(n)$. So one usually assumes $n \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$.
- $\mathbb Z[\zeta_n]$ is the full ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$, but it rarely has unique factorization of elements; ideals are needed.

- Characters of the Galois group $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$ are the [[dirichlet-characters]] modulo $n$. The [[dedekind-zeta]] function of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ is the product of the $L$-functions $L(s, \chi)$ of the primitive characters inducing the characters modulo $n$, and its pole at $s = 1$ is one route to $L(1, \chi) \ne 0$ and Dirichlet's theorem (see [[l-functions]]).
- Gauss and Jacobi sums are elements of cyclotomic fields; see [[gauss-sums]] and [[cubic-characters]].
- Class numbers of cyclotomic fields measure the failure of unique factorization studied in [[class-group]].
- The proofs above use the arithmetic of [[finite-fields]] and the language of [[galois]] theory.
